primitives.name: Judgmental Forecasting
primitives.verbatim_quote: While previously judgement was thought to be the enemy of accuracy, today judgement is recognised as an indispensable component of forecasting and much research attention has been directed at understanding and improving its use.
primitives.assumptions: No domain knowledge available to the forecaster.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Singularity occurs when judgmental forecasts are perfectly consistent across multiple forecasters.

layer2.mapping: Maps judgmental forecasts to a probabilistic distribution within GSI's conformal prediction framework, where empirical verification metrics are derived from historical judgmental performance.
layer2.telemetry: Variance of judgmental forecast errors relative to statistical models serves as the primary verification metric.

primitives.name: Judgmental Bias
primitives.verbatim_quote: Human judgement can be demonstrated to provide a significant benefit to forecasting accuracy but it can also be subject to many biases.
primitives.assumptions: Bias arises from cognitive heuristics such as anchoring, availability, and representativeness.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Bias becomes negligible when forecasters apply calibration techniques or receive feedback.

layer2.mapping: Bias correction algorithms in GSI adjust probability forecasts to account for systematic deviations, aligning with the concept of calibrated judgmental reasoning.
layer2.telemetry: Bias metrics include mean absolute error (MAE) between judgmental and actual outcomes, and calibration scores.

primitives.name: Unmodeled Time Series Component
primitives.verbatim_quote: Towards an understanding of domain knowledge We define domain knowledge as any information relevant to the forecasting task other than the time series—i.e., non-time series information.

reasoning_traces.think: Chapter window 4 explores foundational elements of judgmental forecasting, particularly how confidence, feedback, and ideological frameworks shape prediction accuracy. The interplay between these factors is modeled through probabilistic lenses such as the Brier score and calibration error. These constructs form the basis for GSI’s Bayesian inference engine by enabling dynamic belief revision and uncertainty quantification. Meanwhile, GSE leverages these insights to simulate agent behavior under varying degrees of cognitive load and feedback intensity. The chapter emphasizes that forecasting performance is not merely a function of data but also of the mental models and biases inherent in the forecaster. This aligns with the broader theoretical framework of cognitive science and behavioral economics, where judgmental forecasting is viewed as a complex interaction between domain knowledge, heuristics, and environmental cues. The focus on calibration and refinement provides a structured approach to evaluating forecast quality, which is essential for both risk management and strategic decision-making in high-stakes environments.
